title: Hans im Glück
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 1, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 83. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). 1857 spelling preserved exactly.
about: KHM 83, the most famous of the Grimms’ downward-trade tales. Paid for seven years’ service with a lump of gold the size of his head, Hans sets off home and swaps it away by stages — gold for a horse, horse for a cow, cow for a pig, pig for a goose, goose for a grindstone and a rough field-stone — delighted at every step to be rid of the last burden, until the stones drop into a well and he runs home to his mother with nothing at all, thanking God for the mercy. Whether the tale is laughing at him or agreeing with him it never says. Spelling follows the 1857 edition (daß, gieng, fieng, Thier, ward, Noth).

sentences.t: Hans hatte sieben Jahre bei seinem Herrn gedient, da sprach er zu ihm „Herr, meine Zeit ist herum, nun wollte ich gerne wieder heim zu meiner Mutter, gebt mir meinen Lohn.“
sentences.l: Hans had served seven years with his master, then he spoke to him “Master, my time is up, now I would gladly [go] home again to my mother, give me my wages.”
sentences.i: Hans had served his master seven years; then he said to him: “Master, my time is up. Now I should like to go home again to my mother — give me my wages.”
sentences.n: sprach is the old narrative preterite of sprechen, the ordinary verb of speech in these tales. “meine Zeit ist herum” = my time has run round, i.e. my term of service is out. gebt is a plural imperative: the servant addresses his master as ihr, the older respectful form. German lets a modal stand without its verb of motion — “wollte ich … heim” — so the English has to supply [go].

sentences.t: Der Herr antwortete „du hast mir treu und ehrlich gedient, wie der Dienst war, so soll der Lohn sein,“ und gab ihm ein Stück Gold, das so groß als Hansens Kopf war.
sentences.l: The master answered “you have served me faithfully and honestly; as the service was, so shall the wages be,” and gave him a piece of gold that was as big as Hans’s head.
sentences.i: The master answered: “You have served me faithfully and honestly; as the service was, so shall the reward be” — and he gave him a lump of gold as big as Hans’s head.
sentences.n: “wie …, so …” is the old proportional pair: as the one was, so the other shall be. Hansens is the old genitive of a personal name in -ens. so groß als stands where modern German says so groß wie.

sentences.t: Hans zog sein Tüchlein aus der Tasche, wickelte den Klumpen hinein, setzte ihn auf die Schulter und machte sich auf den Weg nach Haus.
sentences.l: Hans drew his little cloth out of his pocket, wrapped the lump in it, set it on his shoulder and made himself on the way toward home.
sentences.i: Hans drew his kerchief out of his pocket, wrapped the lump in it, set it on his shoulder and set off for home.
sentences.n: “sich auf den Weg machen” = to set out; the reflexive sich cannot be translated on its own. Tüchlein is the diminutive of Tuch, a cloth for bundling things.

sentences.t: Wie er so dahin gieng und immer ein Bein vor das andere setzte, kam ihm ein Reiter in die Augen, der frisch und fröhlich auf einem muntern Pferd vorbei trabte.
sentences.l: As he walked along so and kept setting one leg before the other, a rider came into his eyes, who trotted past brisk and cheerful on a lively horse.
sentences.i: As he went trudging along, setting one leg before the other, a rider came into view, trotting past brisk and merry on a lively horse.
sentences.n: gieng is the 1857 spelling of ging (gehen). “jemandem in die Augen kommen” = to come into someone’s eyes, i.e. to catch the eye — the German makes the rider, not Hans, the subject.

sentences.t: „Ach,“ sprach Hans ganz laut, „was ist das Reiten ein schönes Ding! da sitzt einer wie auf einem Stuhl, stößt sich an keinen Stein, spart die Schuh, und kommt fort, er weiß nicht wie.“
sentences.l: “Ah,” spoke Hans quite loud, “what a fine thing riding is! there one sits as if on a chair, knocks against no stone, spares one’s shoes, and gets on, he knows not how.”
sentences.i: “Ah,” said Hans right out loud, “what a fine thing riding is! You sit there as if on a chair, you knock against no stone, you save your shoes, and on you go, you know not how.”
sentences.n: “was ist das … ein schönes Ding” is the exclamatory order: what a fine thing that is. einer is the indefinite “one”, which German then carries on with er; English switches to “you”. Schuh is the old plural without an ending.

sentences.t: Der Reiter, der das gehört hatte, hielt an und rief „ei, Hans, warum laufst du auch zu Fuß?“
sentences.l: The rider, who had heard that, drew up and called “ei, Hans, why do you go on foot at all?”
sentences.i: The rider, who had heard this, stopped and called: “Why, Hans, what are you doing on foot?”
sentences.n: anhalten is separable — hielt … an. laufen in these tales is simply to walk, to go, not to run. The little word auch in a question adds a shade of “of all things”.

sentences.t: „Ich muß ja wohl,“ antwortete er, „da habe ich einen Klumpen heim zu tragen: es ist zwar Gold, aber ich kann den Kopf dabei nicht gerad halten, auch drückt mirs auf die Schulter.“
sentences.l: “I must indeed,” he answered, “here I have a lump to carry home: it is gold, to be sure, but I cannot hold my head straight with it, and it presses me on the shoulder too.”
sentences.i: “I have to,” he answered; “I have this lump to carry home. It is gold, true enough, but I cannot hold my head straight for it, and it weighs on my shoulder besides.”
sentences.n: haben with zu and an infinitive expresses obligation: “zu tragen haben” = to have to carry. zwar … aber = to be sure … but. mirs = mir es, and the dative mir marks the person affected: it presses on the shoulder to me, i.e. on my shoulder.

sentences.t: „Weißt du was,“ sagte der Reiter, „wir wollen tauschen: ich gebe dir mein Pferd, und du gibst mir deinen Klumpen.“
sentences.l: “Do you know what,” said the rider, “we will trade: I give you my horse, and you give me your lump.”
sentences.i: “Do you know what,” said the rider, “let us trade: I give you my horse and you give me your lump.”
sentences.n: “wir wollen …” is the ordinary German for let us — wollen proposes here, it does not predict.

sentences.t: „Von Herzen gern,“ sprach Hans, „aber ich sage euch ihr müßt euch damit schleppen.“
sentences.l: “From the heart gladly,” spoke Hans, “but I tell you, you will have to drag yourself along with it.”
sentences.i: “With all my heart,” said Hans, “but I tell you, you will have hard work to lug it along.”
sentences.n: “von Herzen gern” = most gladly, a fixed phrase. Hans answers with ihr, the respectful plural, while the rider says du to him — the difference of station is audible all through the tale. “sich schleppen mit” = to lug oneself along with.

sentences.t: Der Reiter stieg ab, nahm das Gold und half dem Hans hinauf, gab ihm die Zügel fest in die Hände und sprach „wenns nun recht geschwind soll gehen, so mußt du mit der Zunge schnalzen, und hopp hopp rufen.“
sentences.l: The rider climbed down, took the gold and helped Hans up, gave him the reins firmly into his hands and spoke “if it is now to go really fast, then you must click with your tongue and call hopp hopp.”
sentences.i: The rider got down, took the gold and helped Hans up, put the reins firmly into his hands and said: “If you want it to go really fast, you must click your tongue and call hopp, hopp.”
sentences.n: absteigen is separable — stieg … ab. “dem Hans” with an article before a name is colloquial and southern, and still living speech. wenns = wenn es; the impersonal “wenn es soll gehen” = if things are to go.

sentences.t: Hans war seelenfroh, als er auf dem Pferde saß und so frank und frei dahin ritt.
sentences.l: Hans was soul-glad when he sat on the horse and rode along so frank and free.
sentences.i: Hans was overjoyed as he sat on the horse and rode along so free and easy.
sentences.n: seelenfroh, soul-glad, is one of those compounds whose first element is pure intensifier. “frank und frei” is a fixed alliterating pair; frank, unhindered, survives only in it. Pferde carries the old dative -e.

sentences.t: Über ein Weilchen fiels ihm ein, es sollte noch schneller gehen, und fieng an mit der Zunge zu schnalzen und hopp hopp zu rufen.
sentences.l: After a little while it occurred to him it should go faster still, and he began to click with his tongue and to call hopp hopp.
sentences.i: After a little while the thought struck him that it should go faster still, and he began clicking his tongue and calling hopp, hopp.
sentences.n: “es fällt mir ein” = it occurs to me — einfallen, separable, with the person in the dative; fiels = fiel es. fieng is the 1857 spelling of fing.

sentences.t: Das Pferd setzte sich in starken Trab, und ehe sichs Hans versah, war er abgeworfen und lag in einem Graben, der die Äcker von der Landstraße trennte.
sentences.l: The horse set itself into a strong trot, and before Hans was aware of it, he was thrown off and lay in a ditch that separated the fields from the highway.
sentences.i: The horse fell into a stiff trot, and before Hans knew what was happening he was thrown and lay in a ditch that divided the fields from the highroad.
sentences.n: “ehe sichs jemand versieht” = before one knows it, a fixed reflexive idiom; sichs = sich es. abwerfen is separable, here in the participle abgeworfen.

sentences.t: Das Pferd wäre auch durchgegangen, wenn es nicht ein Bauer aufgehalten hätte, der des Weges kam und eine Kuh vor sich her trieb.
sentences.l: The horse would have bolted too, if a peasant had not stopped it, who came along the way and drove a cow before him.
sentences.i: The horse would have bolted as well, had a peasant not stopped it — one who was coming along the road driving a cow before him.
sentences.n: durchgehen of a horse = to bolt. “des Weges kommen” is an old genitive of the road travelled: to come along the way. wäre … durchgegangen and hätte … aufgehalten are the past subjunctive of an unreal condition.

sentences.t: Hans suchte seine Glieder zusammen und machte sich wieder auf die Beine.
sentences.l: Hans gathered his limbs together and got himself back on his legs.
sentences.i: Hans collected his limbs and got back on his feet.
sentences.n: zusammensuchen is separable: to search out and gather together — comically applied here to his own limbs. “sich auf die Beine machen” = to get oneself up and going.

sentences.t: Er war aber verdrießlich und sprach zu dem Bauer „es ist ein schlechter Spaß, das Reiten, zumal, wenn man auf so eine Mähre geräth wie diese, die stößt und einen herabwirft, daß man den Hals brechen kann;
sentences.l: But he was out of humour and spoke to the peasant “it is a poor joke, this riding, especially when one lands on such a nag as this one, which jolts you and throws you down so that you can break your neck;
sentences.i: But he was out of humour, and said to the peasant: “Riding is a poor joke, especially when you come by such a nag as this, which jolts you and throws you down so that you may break your neck.
sentences.n: geräth (modern gerät, from gerathen) = to get into, to end up with, by chance rather than by choice. daß here introduces a result: so that. einen is the accusative of the indefinite man, which English turns into “you”.

sentences.t: ich setze mich nun und nimmermehr wieder auf.
sentences.l: I set myself up [on a horse] now and nevermore again.
sentences.i: I shall never mount again as long as I live.
sentences.n: “nun und nimmermehr” is a fixed emphatic phrase for never again; the nun is not a real “now”. sich aufsetzen here is to mount, the separable auf at the end; the literal supplies [on a horse], which the German leaves to the situation. The present tense stands for the future, as German commonly lets it.

sentences.t: Da lob ich mir eure Kuh, da kann einer mit Gemächlichkeit hinter her gehen und hat obendrein seine Milch, Butter und Käse jeden Tag gewiß.
sentences.l: There I praise myself your cow: there one can walk behind at one’s ease and has besides his milk, butter and cheese sure every day.
sentences.i: Now, your cow — there is the thing for me: a man can walk behind her at his ease, and has his milk, butter and cheese certain every day into the bargain.
sentences.n: “da lob ich mir …” is a set expression of preference: that is the thing for me. Gemächlichkeit is unhurried comfort, from gemach, slowly.

sentences.t: Was gäb ich darum, wenn ich so eine Kuh hätte!“
sentences.l: What would I give for it, if I had such a cow!”
sentences.i: What would I not give to have such a cow!”
sentences.n: gäb (for gäbe) and hätte are past subjunctives of a wish. darum = for that, um folded together with the pronoun.

sentences.t: „Nun,“ sprach der Bauer, „geschieht euch so ein großer Gefallen, so will ich euch wohl die Kuh für das Pferd vertauschen.“
sentences.l: “Well,” spoke the peasant, “if so great a favour is done you, then I will gladly trade you the cow for the horse.”
sentences.i: “Well,” said the peasant, “if it is so great a kindness to you, I am willing enough to trade you the cow for the horse.”
sentences.n: A conditional with no wenn: the verb comes first — “geschieht euch …” — and English must supply the “if”. The person favoured stands in the dative, euch. wohl softens: readily enough.

sentences.t: Hans willigte mit tausend Freuden ein: der Bauer schwang sich aufs Pferd und ritt eilig davon.
sentences.l: Hans consented with a thousand joys: the peasant swung himself onto the horse and rode hastily away.
sentences.i: Hans agreed with a thousand thanks; the peasant swung himself onto the horse and rode off in haste.
sentences.n: einwilligen is separable — willigte … ein. “mit tausend Freuden” = most gladly. davonreiten is separable too, and leaves davon at the end.

sentences.t: Hans trieb seine Kuh ruhig vor sich her und bedachte den glücklichen Handel.
sentences.l: Hans drove his cow quietly before him and thought over the lucky bargain.
sentences.i: Hans drove his cow quietly on before him, turning the lucky bargain over in his mind.
sentences.n: “vor sich her treiben” = to drive along in front of oneself; the her marks the motion as seen from the driver. bedenken = to consider, to ponder.

sentences.t: „Hab ich nur ein Stück Brot, und daran wird mirs doch nicht fehlen, so kann ich, so oft mirs beliebt, Butter und Käse dazu essen;
sentences.l: “If I only have a piece of bread — and that surely will not be lacking to me — then I can eat butter and cheese with it as often as it pleases me;
sentences.i: “If only I have a piece of bread — and I shall hardly go short of that — I can eat butter and cheese with it as often as I please.
sentences.n: Another wenn-less conditional: “Hab ich nur …” = if only I have. “es fehlt mir an etwas” = I lack something, the person in the dative — here daran … mirs. belieben also takes the dative: as often as it pleases me.

sentences.t: hab ich Durst, so melk ich meine Kuh und trinke Milch.
sentences.l: if I am thirsty, then I milk my cow and drink milk.
sentences.i: if I am thirsty, I milk my cow and drink milk.
sentences.n: German has thirst — “Durst haben” — where English is thirsty. The verb-first conditional again, its main clause opened by so.

sentences.t: Herz, was verlangst du mehr?“
sentences.l: Heart, what more do you demand?”
sentences.i: Heart, what more could you ask?”
sentences.n: Addressing one’s own heart — “Herz, was verlangst du mehr?” — is a common turn in these tales, half proverb and half exclamation. verlangen = to demand, to ask for.

sentences.t: Als er zu einem Wirthshaus kam, machte er Halt, aß in der großen Freude alles, was er bei sich hatte, sein Mittags- und Abendbrot, rein auf, und ließ sich für seine letzten paar Heller ein halbes Glas Bier einschenken.
sentences.l: When he came to an inn, he made a halt, ate up clean in his great joy everything that he had with him, his midday and evening bread, and had half a glass of beer poured out for himself for his last few Heller.
sentences.i: When he came to an inn he made a halt, and in his great joy ate up clean everything he had with him, his dinner and his supper both, and for his last few pence had half a glass of beer poured for him.
sentences.n: aufessen is separable and its prefix waits to the end — aß … rein auf, ate clean up. Wirthshaus is the 1857 spelling of Wirtshaus. A Heller was the smallest copper coin, so this is the last of his pennies. “sich einschenken lassen” = to have a drink poured for one.

sentences.t: Dann trieb er seine Kuh weiter, immer nach dem Dorfe seiner Mutter zu.
sentences.l: Then he drove his cow onward, always toward his mother’s village.
sentences.i: Then he drove his cow on, always in the direction of his mother’s village.
sentences.n: “nach … zu” is a two-part phrase of direction, with the zu held back to the end: in the direction of. Dorfe has the old dative -e.

sentences.t: Die Hitze ward drückender, je näher der Mittag kam, und Hans befand sich in einer Heide, die wohl noch eine Stunde dauerte.
sentences.l: The heat grew more oppressive the nearer midday came, and Hans found himself on a heath that lasted a good hour more.
sentences.i: The heat grew more oppressive as midday drew nearer, and Hans found himself on a heath that would take a good hour yet to cross.
sentences.n: ward is the old preterite of werden, modern wurde. A heath measured in hours is measured by walking time — an hour of heath still to cross.

sentences.t: Da ward es ihm ganz heiß, so daß ihm vor Durst die Zunge am Gaumen klebte.
sentences.l: Then it grew quite hot to him, so that his tongue stuck to his palate for thirst.
sentences.i: Then he grew very hot, so that his tongue clung to the roof of his mouth for thirst.
sentences.n: “mir ist heiß” = I am hot, with the person in the dative and es as the grammatical subject. “ihm … die Zunge” is the dative of possession: German marks whose tongue it is with a dative rather than a possessive. vor Durst = for thirst, vor giving the cause.

sentences.t: „Dem Ding ist zu helfen,“ dachte Hans, „jetzt will ich meine Kuh melken und mich an der Milch laben.“
sentences.l: “That thing is to be helped,” thought Hans, “now I will milk my cow and refresh myself on the milk.”
sentences.i: “That is easily mended,” thought Hans; “now I will milk my cow and refresh myself with the milk.”
sentences.n: sein + zu + infinitive is a passive of possibility: the thing can be helped. helfen governs the dative, hence dem Ding. “sich an etwas laben” = to refresh oneself on something.

sentences.t: Er band sie an einen dürren Baum, und da er keinen Eimer hatte, so stellte er seine Ledermütze unter, aber wie er sich auch bemühte, es kam kein Tropfen Milch zum Vorschein.
sentences.l: He bound her to a withered tree, and since he had no pail, he set his leather cap underneath; but however he exerted himself, not a drop of milk came to view.
sentences.i: He tied her to a withered tree, and since he had no pail he set his leather cap underneath; but however hard he tried, not a drop of milk appeared.
sentences.n: “wie er sich auch bemühte” — wie … auch = however much, a concessive. “zum Vorschein kommen” = to come to light, to appear. unterstellen is separable, its prefix at the end.

sentences.t: Und weil er sich ungeschickt dabei anstellte, so gab ihm das ungeduldige Thier endlich mit einem der Hinterfüße einen solchen Schlag vor den Kopf, daß er zu Boden taumelte und eine zeitlang sich gar nicht besinnen konnte wo er war.
sentences.l: And because he set about it clumsily, the impatient beast at last gave him such a blow on the head with one of its hind feet that he reeled to the ground and for a time could not recollect at all where he was.
sentences.i: And because he set about it so clumsily, the impatient beast at last dealt him such a kick on the head with one of its hind feet that he reeled to the ground and for a while could not think where he was.
sentences.n: “sich anstellen” = to set about a thing, to go at it — separable, prefix at the end. Thier is the 1857 spelling of Tier. “sich besinnen” = to collect one’s wits, to recall.

sentences.t: Glücklicherweise kam gerade ein Metzger des Weges, der auf einem Schubkarren ein junges Schwein liegen hatte.
sentences.l: Luckily a butcher came just then along the way, who had a young pig lying on a wheelbarrow.
sentences.i: Luckily a butcher came along the road just then, with a young pig lying on his barrow.
sentences.n: “des Weges kommen” again, the old genitive of the road one travels. “liegen haben” = to have something lying, haben with a bare infinitive.

sentences.t: „Was sind das für Streiche!“ rief er und half dem guten Hans auf.
sentences.l: “What sort of tricks are these!” he cried, and helped the good Hans up.
sentences.i: “What kind of goings-on are these!” he cried, and helped good Hans to his feet.
sentences.n: “was für …” = what sort of. aufhelfen is separable and puts the person helped in the dative. Streiche are pranks or tricks — the butcher means, what is all this.

sentences.t: Hans erzählte was vorgefallen war.
sentences.l: Hans told what had happened.
sentences.n: vorfallen = to occur, to happen, separable. The 1857 text prints no comma before was, and the punctuation stands as printed.

sentences.t: Der Metzger reichte ihm seine Flasche und sprach „da trinkt einmal und erholt euch.
sentences.l: The butcher handed him his flask and spoke “here, drink once and recover yourselves.
sentences.i: The butcher held out his flask and said: “Here, take a drink and get your strength back.
sentences.n: trinkt and erholt are plural imperatives — the butcher too addresses Hans as ihr. einmal in an imperative merely softens it: go on and drink. “sich erholen” = to recover oneself.

sentences.t: Die Kuh will wohl keine Milch geben, das ist ein altes Thier, das höchstens noch zum Ziehen taugt oder zum Schlachten.“
sentences.l: The cow will surely give no milk; that is an old beast, which at most is still good for drawing or for slaughtering.”
sentences.i: The cow will give no milk, depend upon it; she is an old beast, fit at most for hauling now, or for the knife.”
sentences.n: wollen with an animal or a thing as subject is the old “will not, refuses to”, not a wish. “zum Ziehen”, “zum Schlachten” — infinitives made into nouns with zu dem: for drawing, for slaughtering. taugen = to be fit for.

sentences.t: „Ei, ei,“ sprach Hans, und strich sich die Haare über den Kopf, „wer hätte das gedacht!
sentences.l: “Ei, ei,” spoke Hans, and stroked his hair back over his head, “who would have thought that!
sentences.i: “Well, well,” said Hans, stroking his hair back over his head, “who would have thought it!
sentences.n: “sich die Haare … streichen” is the dative of possession once more: the sich says whose hair. hätte … gedacht is the past subjunctive of the unreal past.

sentences.t: es ist freilich gut, wenn man so ein Thier ins Haus abschlachten kann, was gibts für Fleisch!
sentences.l: it is certainly good if one can slaughter such a beast for the house — what meat that gives!
sentences.i: it is a fine thing, to be sure, when a man can slaughter such a beast for the household — what meat there is on it!
sentences.n: “ins Haus” means for the household’s own use. “was gibts für Fleisch” is the exclamatory was … für again; gibts = gibt es. abschlachten is separable.

sentences.t: aber ich mache mir aus dem Kuhfleisch nicht viel, es ist mir nicht saftig genug.
sentences.l: but I make myself not much of beef; it is not juicy enough for me.
sentences.i: but I do not think much of beef; it is not juicy enough for my taste.
sentences.n: “sich aus etwas nicht viel machen” = to care little for a thing, a fixed idiom with the dative mir. Kuhfleisch, cow-flesh, is plainer than modern Rindfleisch.

sentences.t: Ja, wer so ein junges Schwein hätte! das schmeckt anders, dabei noch die Würste.“
sentences.l: Yes, if one only had such a young pig! that tastes different, and the sausages besides.”
sentences.i: Ah, if a man had such a young pig! That has quite another taste to it, and the sausages into the bargain.”
sentences.n: “wer … hätte!” is a wish in the past subjunctive, with wer standing for “if one”. “das schmeckt anders” = that tastes quite otherwise, i.e. far better.

sentences.t: „Hört, Hans,“ sprach da der Metzger, „euch zu Liebe will ich tauschen und will euch das Schwein für die Kuh lassen.“
sentences.l: “Listen, Hans,” spoke the butcher then, “for love of you I will trade, and will let you have the pig for the cow.”
sentences.i: “Listen, Hans,” said the butcher then, “to oblige you I will trade, and let you have the pig for the cow.”
sentences.n: “euch zu Liebe” = for your sake, out of kindness to you; modern German writes zuliebe after its dative. lassen here = to let someone have.

sentences.t: „Gott lohn euch eure Freundschaft“ sprach Hans, übergab ihm die Kuh, ließ sich das Schweinchen vom Karren losmachen und den Strick, woran es gebunden war, in die Hand geben.
sentences.l: “God reward you for your kindness,” spoke Hans, handed over the cow to him, had the little pig loosed from the barrow and the rope it was tied to given into his hand.
sentences.i: “God reward you for your kindness,” said Hans; and he handed over the cow, had the little pig untied from the barrow and the rope it was fastened to put into his hand.
sentences.n: lohn is the old subjunctive of wishing: may God reward you. Freundschaft here is the kindness done, not friendship in the abstract. “sich etwas machen lassen” = to have a thing done for one; woran = an dem, to which.

sentences.t: Hans zog weiter und überdachte wie ihm doch alles nach Wunsch gienge, begegnete ihm ja eine Verdrießlichkeit, so würde sie doch gleich wieder gut gemacht.
sentences.l: Hans went on and considered how everything went for him according to his wish: if a vexation did meet him, it was at once made good again.
sentences.i: Hans went on his way, thinking over how everything fell out for him just as he wished: if some vexation did meet him, it was made good again directly.
sentences.n: gienge and würde are the subjunctive of reported thought — the tale keeps Hans’s reflection in his own mouth without quoting it. begegnen takes the dative, ihm. ja here concedes: if indeed some vexation did come.

sentences.t: Es gesellte sich danach ein Bursch zu ihm, der trug eine schöne weiße Gans unter dem Arm.
sentences.l: There joined himself to him after that a lad, who carried a fine white goose under his arm.
sentences.i: Presently a lad fell in with him who was carrying a fine white goose under his arm.
sentences.n: “sich zu jemandem gesellen” = to join company with someone. The opening Es is a placeholder that lets the real subject, ein Bursch, come later; English does not copy it.

sentences.t: Sie boten einander die Zeit, und Hans fieng an von seinem Glück zu erzählen und wie er immer so vortheilhaft getauscht hätte.
sentences.l: They offered one another the time, and Hans began to tell of his luck and how he had always traded so advantageously.
sentences.i: They gave each other good day, and Hans began to tell of his good fortune and how he had always traded so much to his profit.
sentences.n: “einander die Zeit bieten” = to bid one another the time of day, to exchange greetings. hätte is the subjunctive of reported speech: as he told it. vortheilhaft is the 1857 spelling of vorteilhaft.

sentences.t: Der Bursch erzählte ihm daß er die Gans zu einem Kindtaufschmaus brächte.
sentences.l: The lad told him that he was bringing the goose to a christening feast.
sentences.i: The lad told him he was taking the goose to a christening feast.
sentences.n: brächte is again the subjunctive of reported speech, standard after a verb of telling, where English simply uses the past. A Kindtaufschmaus is the feast held after a baptism, a substantial village occasion.

sentences.t: „Hebt einmal,“ fuhr er fort, und packte sie bei den Flügeln, „wie schwer sie ist, die ist aber auch acht Wochen lang genudelt worden.
sentences.l: “Just lift,” he continued, and seized her by the wings, “how heavy she is — but then she has been crammed eight weeks long.
sentences.i: “Just take hold,” he went on, seizing her by the wings, “and feel how heavy she is; but then she has been crammed for eight weeks together.
sentences.n: fortfahren = to go on speaking, separable — fuhr … fort. nudeln is to force-feed a goose with pellets of dough (Nudeln), the old way of fattening a bird for the table.

sentences.t: Wer in den Braten beißt, muß sich das Fett von beiden Seiten abwischen.“
sentences.l: Whoever bites into the roast must wipe himself the fat from both sides.”
sentences.i: Whoever bites into that roast will have to wipe the fat from both sides of his mouth.”
sentences.n: The dative sich marks the person affected: he wipes the grease off himself. Wer …, der … is the old relative-conditional — whoever does this, he must.

sentences.t: „Ja,“ sprach Hans, und wog sie mit der einen Hand, „die hat ihr Gewicht, aber mein Schwein ist auch keine Sau.“
sentences.l: “Yes,” spoke Hans, and weighed her with the one hand, “she has her weight — but my pig is no sow either.”
sentences.i: “Yes,” said Hans, weighing her in one hand, “she has her weight to her; but my pig is no common sow either.”
sentences.n: The last clause plays on two words for the one beast: Schwein is the animal, Sau the coarser word, and to say his pig is “no Sau” is to claim it is no ordinary creature. The point is boast rather than logic, and it resists a tidy English: the idiomatic supplies “common” to carry the force the second word has of itself.

sentences.t: Indessen sah sich der Bursch nach allen Seiten ganz bedenklich um, schüttelte auch wohl mit dem Kopf.
sentences.l: Meanwhile the lad looked about himself on all sides quite doubtfully, and shook his head as well.
sentences.i: Meanwhile the lad looked about him on every side very doubtfully, and shook his head besides.
sentences.n: “sich umsehen” = to look about one, separable, the um waiting at the end. wohl here is roughly “indeed, into the bargain”, not “well”. German shakes with the head — mit dem Kopf.

sentences.t: „Hört,“ fieng er darauf an, „mit eurem Schweine mags nicht ganz richtig sein.
sentences.l: “Listen,” he began thereupon, “with your pig it may not be quite right.
sentences.i: “Listen,” he began then, “there may be something not quite right about that pig of yours.
sentences.n: “es ist nicht ganz richtig mit etwas” = there is something wrong about it, often with a hint of foul play. mags = mag es, and mögen here means may, might. Schweine carries the old dative -e.

sentences.t: In dem Dorfe, durch das ich gekommen bin, ist eben dem Schulzen eins aus dem Stall gestohlen worden.
sentences.l: In the village through which I have come, one has just been stolen from the Schulze out of the sty.
sentences.i: In the village I came through, one was stolen from the Schulze’s sty only just now.
sentences.n: The Schulze was the village headman, the peasant who held the lowest office of authority — the worst possible man to rob. The dative dem Schulzen marks the person robbed. eins = ein Schwein, the noun dropped and its neuter gender left in the ending.

sentences.t: Ich fürchte, ich fürchte, ihr habts da in der Hand.
sentences.l: I fear, I fear, you have it there in your hand.
sentences.i: I am afraid, very much afraid, that is the one you have there in your hand.
sentences.n: habts = habt es. The doubled “ich fürchte” is spoken idiom for grave misgiving. The lad, like the rider and the butcher, says ihr to Hans.

sentences.t: Sie haben Leute ausgeschickt, und es wäre ein schlimmer Handel, wenn sie euch mit dem Schwein erwischten: das geringste ist, daß ihr ins finstere Loch gesteckt werdet.“
sentences.l: They have sent people out, and it would be a bad business if they caught you with the pig: the least is that you are put into the dark hole.”
sentences.i: They have sent men out, and it would be an ugly business if they caught you with the pig; the least of it would be that you are thrown into the black hole.”
sentences.n: ausschicken is separable. wäre and erwischten are past subjunctives of an unreal condition. “das finstere Loch” is the village lock-up, the dark cell beneath the town hall.

sentences.t: Dem guten Hans ward bang, „ach Gott,“ sprach er, „helft mir aus der Noth, ihr wißt hier herum bessern Bescheid, nehmt mein Schwein da und laßt mir eure Gans.“
sentences.l: To good Hans it grew anxious — “ah God,” he spoke, “help me out of my need; you know your way better hereabouts; take my pig there and leave me your goose.”
sentences.i: Good Hans grew frightened. “Ah God,” he said, “help me out of this trouble; you know your way about here better than I do — take my pig and leave me your goose.”
sentences.n: “mir wird bang” = I grow afraid, with the person in the dative and no subject at all; ward is the old wurde. Noth is the 1857 spelling of Not. “Bescheid wissen” = to know how things stand, to know one’s way about.

sentences.t: „Ich muß schon etwas aufs Spiel setzen,“ antwortete der Bursche, „aber ich will doch nicht Schuld sein daß ihr ins Unglück gerathet.“
sentences.l: “I must indeed set something at stake,” answered the lad, “but I will not be to blame that you fall into misfortune.”
sentences.i: “I shall be putting something at risk,” answered the lad, “but I will not be the cause of your coming to grief.”
sentences.n: “etwas aufs Spiel setzen” = to put something at stake, a phrase out of gaming. gerathet is the 1857 spelling of geratet (geraten), to get into, to fall into. schon here concedes: admittedly.

sentences.t: Er nahm also das Seil in die Hand und trieb das Schwein schnell auf einen Seitenweg fort: der gute Hans aber gieng, seiner Sorgen entledigt, mit der Gans unter dem Arme der Heimath zu.
sentences.l: So he took the rope in his hand and drove the pig quickly away onto a side path; but good Hans went, rid of his cares, with the goose under his arm toward home.
sentences.i: So he took the rope in his hand and drove the pig off quickly down a side path; but good Hans went on toward home, rid of his cares, with the goose under his arm.
sentences.n: “seiner Sorgen entledigt” takes the genitive: freed of his cares. In “der Heimath zu” the zu follows its noun and makes it a direction: homeward. Heimath is the 1857 spelling of Heimat, and Arme has the old dative -e.

sentences.t: „Wenn ichs recht überlege,“ sprach er mit sich selbst, „habe ich noch Vortheil bei dem Tausch:
sentences.l: “If I consider it rightly,” he spoke with himself, “I have profit still in the exchange:
sentences.i: “When I think it over properly,” he said to himself, “I have the better of the bargain even so:
sentences.n: German speaks with oneself where English speaks to oneself. Vortheil is the 1857 spelling of Vorteil; ichs = ich es.

sentences.t: erstlich den guten Braten, hernach die Menge von Fett, die herausträufeln wird, das gibt Gänsefettbrot auf ein Vierteljahr:
sentences.l: first the good roast, then the quantity of fat that will trickle out — that gives goose-dripping-bread for a quarter of a year:
sentences.i: first the good roast, and then all the fat that will drip out of it, which makes bread and goose-dripping for a quarter of a year;
sentences.n: erstlich … hernach = firstly … after that. Gänsefettbrot is bread spread with goose fat — the poor household’s butter, and a real luxury of taste. herausträufeln is separable.

sentences.t: und endlich die schönen weißen Federn, die laß ich mir in mein Kopfkissen stopfen, und darauf will ich wohl ungewiegt einschlafen.
sentences.l: and finally the fine white feathers — those I will have stuffed into my pillow, and on that I shall fall asleep well enough unrocked.
sentences.i: and last the fine white feathers, which I shall have stuffed into my pillow; and on that I shall fall asleep well enough without being rocked.
sentences.n: “sich etwas stopfen lassen” = to have a thing stuffed for one, the dative mir saying for whom. ungewiegt, unrocked, is Hans’s joke: a child must be rocked to sleep, but such a pillow will do it for him.

sentences.t: Was wird meine Mutter eine Freude haben!“
sentences.l: What a joy my mother will have!”
sentences.i: How glad my mother will be!”
sentences.n: The exclamatory was … eine Freude, the same shape as “was ist das ein schönes Ding” earlier: what a joy my mother will have.

sentences.t: Als er durch das letzte Dorf gekommen war, stand da ein Scheerenschleifer mit seinem Karren, sein Rad schnurrte, und er sang dazu
sentences.l: When he had come through the last village, there stood a scissors-grinder with his cart; his wheel whirred, and he sang to it
sentences.i: When he had come through the last village, there stood a scissors-grinder with his cart; his wheel whirred, and he sang along with it:
sentences.n: Scheere is the 1857 spelling of Schere. A Scheerenschleifer pushed his grinding wheel from village to village, sharpening knives and scissors as he went. schnurren is the whirring hum of the turning stone.

sentences.t:
„ich schleife die Scheere und drehe geschwind,
und hänge mein Mäntelchen nach dem Wind.“
sentences.l:
“I grind the scissors and turn briskly,
and hang my little cloak according to the wind.”
sentences.i:
“I sharpen the scissors and spin them round fast,
and I hang my cloak whichever way the wind blows.”
sentences.n: “den Mantel nach dem Wind hängen” is the proverb for turning with whatever suits — the grinder is cheerfully confessing an easy conscience. The two lines rhyme geschwind with Wind; the English keeps the sense and lets the rhyme go.

sentences.t: Hans blieb stehen und sah ihm zu; endlich redete er ihn an, und sprach „euch gehts wohl, weil ihr so lustig bei eurem Schleifen seid.“
sentences.l: Hans stopped and watched him; at last he addressed him and spoke “things go well with you, since you are so merry at your grinding.”
sentences.i: Hans stood still and watched him; at last he spoke to him and said: “You must be doing well, to be so merry over your grinding.”
sentences.n: “stehen bleiben” = to stop, literally to remain standing. zusehen, which takes the dative, = to watch; anreden = to address; both separable. “es geht mir wohl” = I am doing well, again with the person in the dative; gehts = geht es.

sentences.t: „Ja,“ antwortete der Scheerenschleifer, „das Handwerk hat einen güldenen Boden.
sentences.l: “Yes,” answered the scissors-grinder, “the trade has a golden floor.
sentences.i: “Yes,” answered the scissors-grinder, “a trade has a golden foundation.
sentences.n: “Handwerk hat goldenen Boden” is a proverb: a craft is a sure fortune, it will always keep a man. güldenen is the old form of goldenen.

sentences.t: Ein rechter Schleifer ist ein Mann, der, so oft er in die Tasche greift, auch Geld darin findet.
sentences.l: A proper grinder is a man who, as often as he reaches into his pocket, finds money in it too.
sentences.i: A proper grinder is a man who finds money in his pocket every time he puts his hand in.
sentences.n: “in die Tasche greifen” = to reach into one’s pocket; greifen takes in with the accusative because there is motion into. darin = in it, the preposition folded together with the pronoun.

sentences.t: Aber wo habt ihr die schöne Gans gekauft?“
sentences.l: But where did you buy the fine goose?”

sentences.t: „Die hab ich nicht gekauft, sondern für mein Schwein eingetauscht.“
sentences.l: “That one I did not buy, but traded for my pig.”
sentences.i: “I did not buy her; I traded my pig for her.”
sentences.n: The direction has to be turned round in English: “für mein Schwein eingetauscht” means got in exchange for my pig. sondern is the “but” that follows a negative; eintauschen is separable. What follows now runs the whole tale backwards, one trade undone in each line.

sentences.t: „Und das Schwein?“
sentences.l: “And the pig?”

sentences.t: „Das hab ich für eine Kuh gekriegt.“
sentences.l: “That I got for a cow.”
sentences.i: “I got that for a cow.”
sentences.n: kriegen is the plain colloquial word for to get, beside the more formal bekommen two lines later.

sentences.t: „Und die Kuh?“
sentences.l: “And the cow?”

sentences.t: „Die hab ich für ein Pferd bekommen.“
sentences.l: “That one I got for a horse.”

sentences.t: „Und das Pferd?“
sentences.l: “And the horse?”

sentences.t: „Dafür hab ich einen Klumpen Gold, so groß als mein Kopf, gegeben.“
sentences.l: “For that I gave a lump of gold as big as my head.”
sentences.n: so groß als again for modern so groß wie; dafür = for that, für folded together with the pronoun.

sentences.t: „Und das Gold?“
sentences.l: “And the gold?”

sentences.t: „Ei, das war mein Lohn für sieben Jahre Dienst.“
sentences.l: “Why, that was my wages for seven years’ service.”
sentences.i: “Why, that was my pay for seven years of service.”
sentences.n: Lohn is a servant’s wage, paid at the end of the whole term rather than week by week — which is why seven years come to one lump. Ei is a mild exclamation: why now, well.

sentences.t: „Ihr habt euch jederzeit zu helfen gewußt,“ sprach der Schleifer, „könnt ihrs nun dahin bringen, daß ihr das Geld in der Tasche springen hört, wenn ihr aufsteht, so habt ihr euer Glück gemacht.“
sentences.l: “You have always known how to help yourself,” spoke the grinder, “if you can now bring it so far that you hear the money spring in your pocket when you get up, then you have made your fortune.”
sentences.i: “You have always known how to help yourself,” said the grinder; “if you can bring it so far that you hear the money jingle in your pocket when you get up, then your fortune is made.”
sentences.n: “sich zu helfen wissen” = to know how to manage, to shift for oneself. Another wenn-less conditional: “könnt ihrs …” = if you can. aufstehen is separable, and “sein Glück machen” = to make one’s fortune.

sentences.t: „Wie soll ich das anfangen?“ sprach Hans.
sentences.l: “How shall I set about it?” spoke Hans.
sentences.i: “How am I to set about that?” said Hans.
sentences.n: anfangen here is not to begin but to go about a thing, to manage it — separable, the prefix at the end.

sentences.t: „Ihr müßt ein Schleifer werden, wie ich; dazu gehört eigentlich nichts, als ein Wetzstein, das andere findet sich schon von selbst.
sentences.l: “You must become a grinder, like me; to that belongs really nothing but a whetstone — the rest finds itself of its own accord.
sentences.i: “You must become a grinder, as I am; nothing is really needed for it but a whetstone, and the rest comes of itself.
sentences.n: “dazu gehört …” = for that one needs, literally to that belongs. “sich finden” = to turn up, to come right of itself. müßt is the 1857 spelling of müsst.

sentences.t: Da hab ich einen, der ist zwar ein wenig schadhaft, dafür sollt ihr mir aber auch weiter nichts als eure Gans geben; wollt ihr das?“
sentences.l: Here I have one; it is a little damaged, to be sure, but for it you shall give me nothing further than your goose — will you do that?”
sentences.i: Here I have one; it is a little the worse for wear, to be sure, but then you are to give me nothing for it but your goose. Will you?”
sentences.n: einen stands for einen Wetzstein, the noun dropped and its gender left in the ending. zwar … aber = to be sure … but; dafür = in return for that. sollen here is what is required, not what will happen.

sentences.t: „Wie könnt ihr noch fragen,“ antwortete Hans, „ich werde ja zum glücklichsten Menschen auf Erden;
sentences.l: “How can you still ask,” answered Hans, “I am becoming the happiest man on earth;
sentences.i: “How can you even ask?” answered Hans. “Why, I am becoming the luckiest man on earth;
sentences.n: “zu etwas werden” = to turn into, to become something. ja is the little word of self-evidence: why, of course. auf Erden is an old dative plural that survives in this phrase alone.

sentences.t: habe ich Geld, so oft ich in die Tasche greife, was brauche ich da länger zu sorgen?“ reichte ihm die Gans hin, und nahm den Wetzstein in Empfang.
sentences.l: if I have money as often as I reach into my pocket, what need have I to worry any longer?” — handed him the goose, and took the whetstone in receipt.
sentences.i: if I have money every time I put my hand in my pocket, what more have I to worry about?” And he handed him the goose and took the whetstone.
sentences.n: The wenn-less conditional once more: “habe ich Geld” = if I have money. “brauchen … zu” with an infinitive = to need to; “in Empfang nehmen” = to take receipt of. The narrative resumes inside the same sentence without repeating er, and the English has to supply “he”.

sentences.t: „Nun,“ sprach der Schleifer, und hob einen gewöhnlichen schweren Feldstein, der neben ihm lag, auf, „da habt ihr noch einen tüchtigen Stein dazu, auf dem sichs gut schlagen läßt, und ihr eure alten Nägel gerade klopfen könnt.
sentences.l: “Now,” spoke the grinder, and lifted up an ordinary heavy field-stone that lay beside him, “there you have a good solid stone into the bargain, on which it lets itself beat well, and you can knock your old nails straight.
sentences.i: “Now,” said the grinder, picking up an ordinary heavy field-stone that lay beside him, “there you have a good solid stone into the bargain, one you can hammer on nicely and straighten your old nails on.
sentences.n: aufheben is separable and its prefix waits out the whole relative clause — hob … auf. “auf dem sichs gut schlagen läßt” — sich lassen with an infinitive is a passive of possibility: on which one can beat well. Straightening bent nails for re-use was ordinary household thrift.

sentences.t: Nehmt hin und hebt ihn ordentlich auf.“
sentences.l: Take it and keep it properly.”
sentences.i: Take it, and take good care of it.”
sentences.n: aufheben has two senses and the tale uses both within two lines: to lift up, and to put by, to keep. hinnehmen = to take what is held out. Both are separable, and both here are plural imperatives to Hans.

sentences.t: Hans lud den Stein auf und gieng mit vergnügtem Herzen weiter; seine Augen leuchteten vor Freude, „ich muß in einer Glückshaut geboren sein,“ rief er aus, „alles was ich wünsche trifft mir ein, wie einem Sonntagskind.“
sentences.l: Hans loaded the stone up and went on with a contented heart; his eyes shone for joy. “I must have been born in a luck-skin,” he cried out, “everything I wish comes true for me, as for a Sunday’s child.”
sentences.i: Hans loaded up the stone and went on with a contented heart; his eyes shone with joy. “I must have been born in a caul,” he cried, “everything I wish for comes true, as it does for a Sunday child.”
sentences.n: The Glückshaut is the caul, the membrane a child is now and then born inside, held to bring lifelong luck. A Sonntagskind, born on a Sunday, was thought lucky and able to see what others cannot. eintreffen = to come true, separable; vor Freude = for joy, the vor giving the cause.

sentences.t: Indessen, weil er seit Tagesanbruch auf den Beinen gewesen war, begann er müde zu werden; auch plagte ihn der Hunger, da er allen Vorrath auf einmal in der Freude über die erhandelte Kuh aufgezehrt hatte.
sentences.l: Meanwhile, because he had been on his legs since daybreak, he began to grow tired; hunger plagued him too, since he had eaten up all his provision at one go in his joy over the traded-for cow.
sentences.i: Meanwhile, having been on his legs since daybreak, he began to grow weary; and hunger plagued him too, for he had eaten up his whole store at one go in his joy over the cow he had got.
sentences.n: “auf den Beinen sein” = to be up and about. “die erhandelte Kuh” is an attributive participle — the traded-for cow — which English usually has to unpack into a relative clause. aufzehren = to consume entirely, separable.

sentences.t: Er konnte endlich nur mit Mühe weiter gehen und mußte jeden Augenblick Halt machen; dabei drückten ihn die Steine ganz erbärmlich.
sentences.l: At last he could go on only with effort and had to make a halt every moment; and withal the stones pressed on him quite wretchedly.
sentences.i: At last he could go on only with difficulty and had to halt every moment; and the stones weighed on him miserably besides.
sentences.n: “jeden Augenblick” is an accusative of time with no preposition — every moment. dabei = with that, at the same time. erbärmlich, from Erbarmen, pity, means pitifully, wretchedly.

sentences.t: Da konnte er sich des Gedankens nicht erwehren, wie gut es wäre, wenn er sie gerade jetzt nicht zu tragen brauchte.
sentences.l: Then he could not defend himself against the thought how good it would be if he did not have to carry them just now.
sentences.i: Then he could not put away the thought of how good it would be if he had not to carry them just now.
sentences.n: “sich einer Sache erwehren” takes the genitive — des Gedankens — and means to fend a thing off. wäre and brauchte are past subjunctives of an unreal wish.

sentences.t: Wie eine Schnecke kam er zu einem Feldbrunnen geschlichen, wollte da ruhen und sich mit einem frischen Trunk laben: damit er aber die Steine im Niedersitzen nicht beschädigte, legte er sie bedächtig neben sich auf den Rand des Brunnens.
sentences.l: Like a snail he came creeping to a field-well, meant to rest there and refresh himself with a fresh draught; but so that he should not damage the stones in the sitting down, he laid them carefully beside him on the rim of the well.
sentences.i: He came creeping like a snail to a well in the fields, meaning to rest there and refresh himself with a cool drink; but so as not to damage the stones as he sat down, he laid them carefully beside him on the rim of the well.
sentences.n: “kam geschlichen” — kommen with a past participle is the German for came creeping, came running. damit … nicht is a clause of purpose: so that … not. “im Niedersitzen” is an infinitive used as a noun: in the act of sitting down.

sentences.t: Darauf setzte er sich nieder und wollte sich zum Trinken bücken, da versah ers, stieß ein klein wenig an, und beide Steine plumpten hinab.
sentences.l: Thereupon he sat himself down and was about to bend to drink, when he made a slip, knocked against them a very little, and both stones plumped down.
sentences.i: Then he sat down and was bending to drink, when he made a slip, gave them the slightest knock, and both stones plumped down.
sentences.n: “sich versehen” = to make a slip, to be caught out — the same verb as “ehe sichs Hans versah” when the horse threw him; ers = er es. anstoßen = to knock against, separable. plumpen is the sound-word for a heavy fall into water.

sentences.t: Hans, als er sie mit seinen Augen in die Tiefe hatte versinken sehen, sprang vor Freuden auf, kniete dann nieder und dankte Gott mit Thränen in den Augen daß er ihm auch diese Gnade noch erwiesen und ihn auf eine so gute Art und ohne daß er sich einen Vorwurf zu machen brauchte, von den schweren Steinen befreit hätte, die ihm allein noch hinderlich gewesen wären.
sentences.l: Hans, when he had seen them sink into the depth with his own eyes, sprang up for joy, then knelt down and thanked God with tears in his eyes that he had shown him this mercy too and had freed him, in so good a way and without his needing to reproach himself, from the heavy stones, which alone had still been a hindrance to him.
sentences.i: Hans, when he had seen them sink into the depths with his own eyes, sprang up for joy, then knelt down and thanked God with tears in his eyes for showing him this mercy too, and for freeing him, in so kindly a fashion and with nothing to reproach himself with, of the heavy stones that alone were still in his way.
sentences.n: “hatte versinken sehen” is the double infinitive: where English says had seen them sink, German turns the participle of sehen back into an infinitive and sends both verbs to the end. erwiesen hätte and gewesen wären are the subjunctive of reported thought — this is Hans’s prayer, not the narrator’s claim. “sich einen Vorwurf machen” = to reproach oneself.

sentences.t: „So glücklich wie ich,“ rief er aus, „gibt es keinen Menschen unter der Sonne.“
sentences.l: “So lucky as I,” he cried out, “there is no man under the sun.”
sentences.i: “There is not a man under the sun as lucky as I am,” he cried.
sentences.n: The German puts the comparison first, before the es gibt clause, which English cannot copy — hence the reordering. ausrufen is separable. glücklich is both lucky and happy, and the tale’s title, Hans im Glück, lives on exactly that doubleness.

sentences.t: Mit leichtem Herzen und frei von aller Last sprang er nun fort, bis er daheim bei seiner Mutter war.
sentences.l: With a light heart and free of every burden he now sprang onward, until he was at home with his mother.
sentences.i: With a light heart and free of every burden he now ran on until he was home with his mother.
sentences.n: The tale ends where it began, at his mother’s, and Hans arrives with nothing at all. leichtem Herzen is dative after mit; “frei von” = free of. fortspringen is separable.
